title: Remark
body_md:
In our approach, we view the difference $ 
\left\lVert \Phi(t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2-  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2$ as the limit of continuous functions on $ H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, with $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$. An alternative to give a meaning to this quantity (for $u \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$) could have been to use a \textit{nonlinear smoothing} for the solutions of \eqref{NLS}. In the context of this paper, with $s>\frac{3}{2}$, the result in Theorem 1 from the interesting work \cite{mcconnell_nonlin_smoothing} implies that for  $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$ (close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$), we have the following nonlinear smoothing (for $u \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$):
    \begin{equation*}
       v(t) := \Phi(t)u - e^{it\partial_x^2} e^{-i\frac{3}{2\pi} \int_0^t  
\left\lVert \Phi(\tau)u \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^4}^4 d\tau} u \in \mathcal C([-T,T]; H^{\sigma + 1-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}))
    \end{equation*}
    for $0<\varepsilon < 1$, and at least for small time $T>0$.
    Hence, we could have tried to define the difference $ 
\left\lVert \Phi(t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2-  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2$ as :
    \begin{equation*}
         
\left\lVert \Phi(t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2-  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2 :=  
\left\lVert v(t) \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2 + 2 \textnormal{Re} \bigl \langle \langle \nabla \rangle^{2s - \sigma} v(t),  \langle \nabla \rangle^\sigma \big(e^{it\partial_x^2} e^{-i\frac{3}{2\pi} \int_0^t  
\left\lVert \Phi(\tau)u \right\rVert 
_{\mathbb{L}^4}^4 d\tau} u\big) \bigr \rangle_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})}
    \end{equation*}
    since this formula is true when $u$ is smooth (with $\langle.,. \rangle_{\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})}$ the $\mathbb{L}^2(\mathbb{T})$-scalar product). With $\varepsilon$ close to 0, the $1-\varepsilon$ gain of regularity in the smoothing above implies that for $u \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, $ 
\left\lVert v(t) \right\rVert 
_{H^s(\mathbb{T})}^2<+\infty$ because $\sigma+1-\varepsilon$ is close to $s+\frac{1}{2}>s$. However, this smoothing is not enough to define the term $\langle \nabla \rangle^{2s-\sigma}v(t)$ because $\sigma + 1 - \varepsilon < 2s-\sigma$, no matter how close $\varepsilon$ and $\sigma$ are close to 0 and $s-\frac{1}{2}$ respectively. For  $\langle \nabla \rangle^{2s-\sigma}v(t)$ to be well-defined, we need a gain of $1+ \varepsilon'$ regularity, where $\varepsilon'>0$.

body_md:
\label{rem continuity of the densities}
    For $\sigma < s-\frac{1}{2}$ close enough to $s-\frac{1}{2}$, we deduce from Proposition~\ref{prop R_s,N continuous}, Proposition~\ref{prop continuity of Qs,N and deterministic estimate} (whose proofs are provided in Section~\ref{section Proofs of the deterministic properties}), and from the continuity properties of the flow, that the map :
    \begin{equation*}
        (t,u) \in \mathbb{R} \times H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}) \mapsto \textnormal{exp} \left( R_s(\Phi(-t)u)-R_s(u) -\int_0^{-t} Q_{s,N}(\Phi_N(\tau)u) d\tau\right)
    \end{equation*}
    is continuous, for any $N\in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$. \\
    Moreover, on $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$, the a priori ill-defined object $-\frac{1}{2}( 
\left\lVert \Phi(-t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2- 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2)$ can be seen as the well-defined object:
    \begin{equation*}
        -\frac{1}{2}( 
\left\lVert \Phi(-t)u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2- 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^s}^2) := R_s(\Phi(-t)u)-R_s(u) - \int_0^{-t} Q_{s}(\Phi(\tau)u) d\tau
    \end{equation*}

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A \in \mathcal B(H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T}))$. Let us prove that $\mu(A) = 
u(A)$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. From the inner regularity of $\mu$ (see Proposition ef{prop inner regularity of rho}), we invoke a compact set $K$ of $H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$ such that $K \subset A$ and $\mu(A) - \varepsilon \leq \mu(K)$. Thus,
     egin{equation*}
        \mu(A) - \varepsilon \leq \mu(K) = 
u(K) \leq 
u(A)
    \end{equation*}
    Since $\varepsilon >0$ is arbitrary, we conclude that $\mu(A) \leq 
u(A)$. By interchanging the roles of $\mu$ and $
u$, we obtain the converse inequality.

label: prop exponential bound
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop exponential bound} Let $u_0 \in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{T})$. There exists a constant $C_0 > 0$ only depending on $ 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1(\mathbb{T})}$ and $\sigma\geq 1$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{exponential bound for NLS solution}
     
\left\lVert u(t) \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} e^{C_0|t|}, \hspace{0.1cm} \hspace{0.1cm}\textnormal{for all} \hspace{0.1cm} t \in I_{max}(u_0)
\end{equation}
    and,
\begin{equation}\label{exponential bound for truncated solution}
   ||u_N(t)||_{H^{\sigma}} \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} e^{C_0|t|},  \hspace{0.1cm} \hspace{0.1cm} \textnormal{for all} \hspace{0.1cm} t \in I_{max,N}(u_0)
\end{equation}
where $u$ is the maximal solution of \eqref{NLS} and $u_N$ is the maximal solution of \eqref{truncated equation}. Moreover, we can explicitly choose $C_0 \leq C_{\sigma} (1+  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1(\mathbb{T})})^{12}$ where $C_{\sigma} >0$ depends only on $\sigma$.
head: environment

label: exponential bound, grönwall
title: Proof
body_md:
We use the convention $\Pi_{\infty} = id$, $u_{\infty} = u$ and $I_{max,\infty}(u_0) = I_{max}(u_0)$. Let $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty \}$ and $t \in I_{max,N}(u_0)$. Passing to the $H^{\sigma}$-norm in the Duhamel formula
    \begin{equation*}
        u_N(t) = e^{i(t)\partial_x^2}u_0 -i \int_{0}^t e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}\Pi_N(|\Pi_N u_N(\tau)|^4 \Pi_N u_N(\tau))d\tau
    \end{equation*}
    we get that, for some constant $C>0$ (only depending on $\sigma$),
    \begin{equation}\label{exponential bound, grönwall}
        \begin{split}
            ||u_N(t)||_{H^{\sigma}} & \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} + \mid \int_0^t  
\left\lVert |\Pi_N u_N(\tau)|^4 \Pi_N u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} d\tau\mid \\
            & \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} + C \mid \int_0^t  
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} 
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^4_{W(\mathbb{T})} d\tau \mid 
        \end{split}
    \end{equation}
The crucial point of the proof is that $ 
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{W(\mathbb{T})}$ is bounded by the $H^1(\mathbb{T})$-norm of the initial data. Indeed, using the mass and Hamiltonian conservation 
\begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
         
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{W(\mathbb{T})} & \leq  
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{H^1(\mathbb{T})} \\
        & \leq ( 
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2} +  
\left\lVert \partial_xu_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2})^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
        & \lesssim \left(  
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2} + \left(\frac{1}{2} 
\left\lVert \partial_xu_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2} + \frac{1}{6} 
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
^6_{\mathbb{L}^6}\right) \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
        & \lesssim ( 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2} + \frac{1}{2} 
\left\lVert \partial_xu_0 \right\rVert 
^2_{\mathbb{L}^2} + \frac{1}{6} 
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
^6_{\mathbb{L}^6})^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
        & \leq C'_0
     \end{split}   
\end{equation*}
where we can choose $C'_0 \sim (1 +  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1(\mathbb{T})})^3$, because $H^1(\mathbb{T})$ embeds continuously in $\mathbb{L}^6(\mathbb{T})$. Now, plugging this bound into \eqref{exponential bound, grönwall}, we get 
\begin{equation*}
    ||u_N(t)||_{H^{\sigma}} \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} + C_0 \mid \int_0^t   
\left\lVert u_N(\tau) \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} d\tau \mid
\end{equation*}
where we can choose $C_0 \sim (1 +  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^1(\mathbb{T})})^{12}$. Then, applying Gronwall's inequality, we obtain 
\begin{equation*}
    ||u_N(t)||_{H^{\sigma}} \leq  
\left\lVert u \right\rVert 
_{H^{\sigma}} e^{C_0|t|}
\end{equation*}
which is the desired bound.
